extracted.intended_audience: general public, policymakers, regulators, and researchers interested in the Fukushima accident and nuclear safety/response
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, operational changes, regulatory findings, and policy measures discussed or recommended in the wake of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident, covering evacuation, communication, decontamination, radioactive wastewater treatment, equipment/hardware standards, and regulatory independence. Useful for informing emergency planning, reactor design/retrofit, and post-accident remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evacuation planning for hospitals and nursing facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fukushima accident underscored critical issues regarding the evacuation of hospitals and nursing care facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evacuation plans must explicitly address vulnerable institutions (hospitals, nursing homes), ensuring procedures that minimize loss of life during evacuation (logistics, medical care continuity, transport, sheltering). Consider risks of evacuation itself versus shelter-in-place for these populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and transparent public communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese public felt that the government and TEPCO provided limited information about the accident in the early weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities must provide timely, accurate, and comprehensible information to the public during a nuclear crisis; avoid withholding key facts or delaying disclosure. Expert analyses understandable to laypersons should be offered promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide expert analysis understandable to laypersons
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert analysis of the accident that was understandable to lay-persons was not given by the government or TEPCO, but by Masashi Gotō.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include accessible expert briefings (plain-language explanations of radiological risks, protective actions) to help public understanding and reduce panic or misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper handling and sharing of monitoring data (SPEEDI etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: MEXT only sent data from the SPEEDI network to the Fukushima prefectural government and was later criticized for delaying the communication of data to the U.S. military.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring data should be forwarded promptly to all relevant authorities and, where appropriate, to the public; protocols must exist for rapid inter-agency and international data-sharing to inform evacuation and protective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward monitoring data to regulatory bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The data was not forwarded to the Nuclear Safety Commission, but was made public by the United States on the 23rd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure monitoring and modeling outputs are routed to independent regulatory and oversight bodies to enable coordinated response and oversight; do not silo data within single ministries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intentional concealment of critical terms (e.g., 'core meltdown')
rubrics_metrics.description: TEPCO officials were instructed not to use the phrase 'core meltdown' in order to conceal the meltdown until they officially recognized it two months after the accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit directives that censor or downplay critical technical information. Clear, accurate terminology should be used publicly to maintain trust and enable proper protective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping of key crisis meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government did not keep records of key meetings during the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contemporaneous records (minutes, decisions, attendance) of crisis-management meetings for accountability, post-incident review, and legal/administrative purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on advisory communications (read/respond to urgent emails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emails from the Nuclear and Industrial Safety Agency to the Fukushima prefectural government, including evacuation and health advisories from 12 March 23:54 to 16 March 09:00, went unread and were deleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish procedures to ensure urgent advisory communications are received, acknowledged, and acted upon by responsible personnel; prevent deletion or ignoring of time-sensitive warnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh evacuation harms vs shelter-in-place (months of life lost consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of months of life lost, the loss of life would have been far smaller if all residents had done nothing at all, or were sheltered in place, instead of evacuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evacuation decisions should incorporate quantitative assessments of health outcomes (including months of life lost) and not assume evacuation is always the lesser harm; consider shelter-in-place where appropriate to minimize overall harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mental health impacts in evacuation and relocation decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The psychological consequences are enormous... Relocation is not easy, the stress is very big. We must not only track those problems, but also treat them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency planning and compensation programs must include mental health monitoring, treatment, and social supports; anticipate psychosomatic issues, depression, alcoholism, suicide risk, and family disruption as part of evacuation impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decontamination threshold of 1 millisievert per year
rubrics_metrics.description: The government enacted an order to decontaminate over a hundred areas where the level of additional radiation was greater than one millisievert per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and apply decontamination/remediation thresholds; note this threshold is described as 'much lower' than necessary for protecting health in the text, so choice of thresholds should be justified scientifically and communicated clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of contaminated water (remove radionuclides except tritium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimately the contaminated water, after treatment to remove radionuclides other than tritium, has to be discharged into the Pacific ocean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement water-treatment systems that remove as many radionuclides as practicable; plan for management of tritium (which cannot be separated from water) and base disposal decisions on dose assessments and regulatory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dose calculations to inform water disposal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2020 committee ... calculated that discharging all the water to the sea in one year would cause a radiation dose of 0.81 microsieverts to the local people, whereas evaporation would cause 1.2 microsieverts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base disposal routes (sea discharge vs evaporation) on transparent dose assessments compared to natural background and international guidance; involve independent review (e.g., IAEA) and communicate expected doses to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan interim storage and tank capacity for contaminated water
rubrics_metrics.description: As of October 2019, 1.17 million cubic meters of contaminated water was stored in the plant area... Tanks used to store the water were expected to be filled in 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure long-term storage plans and contingency for tank filling, container degradation, and transfer operations; monitor container integrity and plan timely transfers or treatment to avoid urgent failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address degrading waste containers and slurry transfer urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority warned that some of 3,373 waste storage containers for the radioactive slurry were degrading faster than expected... transferring the slurry to a new container was very time consuming, this posed an urgent problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular inspection and replacement/transfer programs for contaminated waste containers; invest in efficient transfer methods and prioritize urgent degradation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid regulatory capture and conflicts of interest (amakudari)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations... showed the man-made nature of the catastrophe and its roots in regulatory capture associated with a 'network of corruption, collusion, and nepotism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design regulatory frameworks that separate promotion and oversight responsibilities, prevent revolving-door appointments, and ensure independent, empowered nuclear regulators to enforce safety requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea wall adequacy in tsunami-prone areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The most obvious was that in tsunami-prone areas, a power station's sea wall must be adequately tall and robust. At the Onagawa Nuclear Power Plant... the sea wall was 14 meters (46 ft) tall and successfully withstood the tsunami.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sea walls and coastal defenses to credible worst-case tsunami heights based on updated seismic/tsunami studies; use conservative design margins and reassess as new science emerges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Install passive autocatalytic recombiners (PARs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nuclear power station operators around the world began to install passive autocatalytic recombiners ('PARs'), which do not require electricity to operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy PARs to mitigate hydrogen accumulation and reduce risk of hydrogen explosions; place recombiners where hydrogen is likely to collect (e.g., reactor building tops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement Filtered Containment Venting Systems (FCVS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpowered filtering systems on containment building vent lines, known as Filtered Containment Venting Systems (FCVS), can safely catch radioactive materials and thereby allow reactor core depressurization, with steam and hydrogen venting with minimal radioactivity emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider FCVS or equivalent filtration to enable controlled depressurization while minimizing airborne radioactive releases; design filtration systems and, where used, position tanks (external water tanks) appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: External water tank filtration positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Filtration using an external water tank system is the most common established system in European countries, with the water tank positioned outside the containment building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using filtration-by-water-tank systems, consider external placement to reduce contamination risks to containment; evaluate system designs used internationally for best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain 3+ day backup battery supply for Gen II reactors in flood/tsunami areas
rubrics_metrics.description: For Generation II reactors located in flood or tsunami prone areas, a 3+ day supply of back-up batteries has become an informal industry standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide extended-duration uninterruptible power sources sized to maintain essential instrumentation and cooling for at least several days in prolonged station-blackout scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harden backup diesel generator rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Another change is to harden the location of back-up diesel generator rooms with water-tight, blast-resistant doors and heat sinks, similar to those used by nuclear submarines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physically protect generators (elevation, waterproofing, blast resistance, thermal management) to ensure operability after extreme external events such as flooding or explosions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt passive nuclear safety in new reactor designs (Generation III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many constructed Generation III reactors adopt the principle of passive nuclear safety. They take advantage of convection and gravity to ensure an adequate supply of cooling water to handle the decay heat, without the use of pumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate passive safety features that achieve core cooling without active systems or operator actions during loss-of-power scenarios to reduce vulnerability to station blackout conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop robust robotics capable of high-radiation tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The accident illustrated that robots lacked sufficient dexterity and robustness to perform critical tasks. In response... competitions were hosted by DARPA to accelerate development of humanoid robots... a wide variety of specially designed robots were employed... but as of early 2016, three of them had promptly become non-functional due to the intensity of the radioactivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in development and procurement of radiation-hardened, highly dexterous robotic systems able to perform complex tasks in contaminated zones; test robots under realistic conditions and maintain redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct rigorous risk assessment and prepare for collateral damage
rubrics_metrics.description: NAIIC found that TEPCO had failed to meet basic safety requirements such as risk assessment, preparing for containing collateral damage, and developing evacuation plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators must conduct comprehensive risk analyses (including low-probability/high-consequence scenarios), prepare contingency plans to contain collateral damage, and maintain up-to-date, practiced evacuation plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect emergency diesel generators and EDGs from flooding
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission warned of a risk of losing emergency power in 1991... Unit 1 EDG disabled by flooding in 1991.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure EDGs and related emergency power infrastructure are sited/protected to avoid failure from flooding or other site hazards, and that redundant, diverse power sources exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on safety study recommendations regardless of public anxiety concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2000, an in-house TEPCO report recommended safety measures against seawater flooding... TEPCO did not act due to concerns about creating anxieties over the safety of the nuclear power plant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and operator decisions should prioritize implementation of evidence-based safety measures recommended by studies, rather than withholding actions for fear of public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish strict agri-food radionuclide limits and inspection regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional regulatory limits for radionuclides in agri-food products were introduced after Fukushima. These became the world's strictest in 2012.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conservative radionuclide limits for foodstuffs, implement widespread testing and inspection programs, and apply restrictions on shipping/consumption where limits are exceeded to protect public health and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make urgent, transparent decisions on treated-water disposal with independent review
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2020 committee... concluded that the purified water should be released to the sea or evaporated... IAEA recommended that a decision on the water disposal must be made urgently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize timely, transparent decisions on disposal of treated water, supported by independent technical review (e.g., IAEA), clear communication of expected doses, and stakeholder engagement to manage reputational and socio-economic impacts.
